prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat bands at a magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in this tunable moire system

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from the two-part B005 plus B046 to B046 alone, with Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer. My reason is not a change in how I rank the science. It is that the first round showed me my two-part design was bought with a credit compromise I cannot defend. Spending three seats across two achievements forced me to drop Bistritzer from the 2011 prediction, and to leave IceCube with one name for a collaboration-scale detector. Twisted bilayer graphene is the case in which I can identify the clue from nature most clearly among the candidates the committee can plausibly agree on: a quantitative prediction of flat bands at a magic angle, then an experiment in 2018 that found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle, then wide reproduction and imaging by independent groups in several moire systems. All eight of us ranked it in the opening and five of us name it as first alternative, which I do not treat as merit in itself, but it tells me the disagreement is about credit and timing, not about whether nature said something. The discovery here is that a single tunable device moves between metal, correlated insulator and superconductor, and that does not depend on the pairing mechanism being settled. We gave the 2013 prize for the Higgs mechanism after the particle and the 1987 prize for high-temperature superconductivity within a year of the discovery, long before anyone could explain the pairing, so an unsettled mechanism is not by itself a reason to wait.
statement.case_against: Two reservations remain and I will not hide them. First, eight years is young, and if the pairing mechanism ends up being something unexpected the citation wording about superconducting states will still hold, but a sceptic could say the committee acted before the physics was understood. I keep the citation on the discovery of the states and not on their explanation for that reason. Second, three names cannot carry the full history. Andrei's STM work from 2010 showed twist-dependent van Hove singularities and flat-band signatures early, Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto had an earlier continuum model, and Cao, Fatemi and the other 2018 co-authors did much of the bench work. I choose Bistritzer over Andrei because the 2011 prediction is a specific, quantitative, falsifiable statement with two authors, whereas Andrei's evidence is real but did not predict the correlated phases. I accept that this is a judgement the condensed-matter members should test, not one I can settle from my own field. I also accept that I am dropping IceCube, which I still regard as the most direct discovery by detector on the list, because I cannot defend a one-name award for it from the supplied credits.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B046 alone with Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer, would not wait for the pairing mechanism, and still flags Andrei, Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto as unresolved attribution questions.
responses.response: I now stand with you on the slate and on the maturity argument, and I said in round 1 that I would revert to this trio if B046 stood alone. I should be exact about why I do not choose Andrei: her 2010 STM results are a genuine early signature of flat-band physics, but they observed van Hove singularities and did not predict or find the correlated and superconducting phases, which is what the citation is about. I would like you to tell us, as the condensed-matter expert, whether you think the earlier continuum-model theory of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto weakens Bistritzer's claim. If you think it does, then a three-person prize has a priority problem and I would want to hear it before the ballot, not after.

responses.point: Mehlig supports Kane, Mele and Molenkamp for B028 on a simple Z2 mechanism confirmed in HgTe, but concedes the HgTe edge conductance fell short of perfect quantisation and that a slate with Hasan would be at least as defensible.
responses.response: Your own concession is what makes me hesitate. When the sceptic can call the experimental half thin and the 3D strand through Hasan is called the more consequential by many in the field, then the nature-said-something test is less clean than for twisted graphene, where the transport experiment showed the effect directly and many groups saw it again. I still regard B028 as the safest mature outcome and it is my first alternative, and I thank you for being candid that it can be built on two slates. I remain unconvinced that a second topological prize two years after 2016 needs less justification than the one you give, namely symmetry-protected band topology in real materials as against phase transitions in model systems. That distinction is fair, but it is a distinction a citation would have to carry.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first and accepts that a one-person award is open to criticism, but prefers B028 as the candidate the committee can actually agree on, with B046 and B005 as alternatives.
responses.response: You answered my round-1 question about whether I would defend a solo IceCube prize more generously than I did myself. I argued that Halzen's concept and leadership trace the achievement to a person, but with AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal and the collaboration on the other side and only Halzen in the supplied names, I cannot make that defence strong enough for a final ballot, and I would sooner say that than push my favourite. I keep B005 as my first alternative so that it stays on the table if the committee finds a credit formulation I cannot, and I would ask you, as the person closest to astroparticle physics, whether any name beyond Halzen is defensible in your view. If not, I think we should both accept that the strongest scientific case on our side of the table is not yet a prize we can name.

responses.point: Kroll and Lindroth prefer B034 with Katori and Ye, arguing the attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist and that reproduction in several laboratories settles maturity.
responses.response: I accept your argument on attribution and reproduction and I do not dispute the 10^-18 performance. My round-1 question stands unanswered, though: you list gravitational redshift over millimetres, constraints on varying constants, dark matter searches and geodesy, and as far as I can tell these are capabilities and limits, not a finding that surprised us. The strongest honest version of your case is the redefinition of the second, which has not happened. I would be more persuaded if the committee waited for that, or if you can name one result from the lattice clocks that changed what we believe about nature. Until then I rank it below the moire candidate, though I fully recognise that a clock is a stronger instrument of discovery than my own theoretical background lets me judge.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B028 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp and values the agreement between band-structure calculations and measured spectra, but concedes that the credit is contested and the trio is defensible and not unique.
responses.response: I respect the argument that theory and measured spectra agree quantitatively, and as a string theorist I am the last person to complain about a calculation that works. I would add that this agreement exists for the moire case too, in the sense that the continuum model predicted a magic angle and the flat-band behaviour was later imaged by scanning probes. We differ on how much weight the credit problem should carry. You and I both name Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D strand as left out, and I think a prize where we can name the omissions in advance is a prize where the committee has to explain itself afterwards. For B046 the omissions are Andrei and some earlier theorists, which is a smaller and more local problem, although it is not zero.

uncertainties: Whether Bistritzer rather than Andrei is the right third name, and how much the earlier continuum-model theory of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto weakens a two-author attribution of the 2011 prediction; this is a condensed-matter judgement I defer to colleagues on.
Whether eight years and an unsettled pairing mechanism make B046 premature, and whether the committee prefers to wait, which would push the committee toward B028.
Whether the committee finds a defensible way to credit IceCube, which I currently cannot do with only Halzen supplied and so have placed as an alternative.

Whether B028 is sufficiently distinct from the 2016 prize and whether the 2D quantum spin Hall and 3D topological insulator strands can be covered by one trio; I would not oppose B028 if B046 fails to win support.
My recollection of IceCube source-association and priority details and of the early moire literature is from memory and has not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for any shortlisted candidate. My ties are to David Gross, my PhD supervisor, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala string group, none of whom is connected to a shortlisted name. I work in string theory and cosmology and am not a specialist in condensed matter or neutrino detectors, so on B046 and B028 I defer to the condensed-matter members on technical detail. As Secretary I have a procedural role in the process, but that is not a conflict regarding any candidate. This disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
